pattern: Stateful connection tier + stateless routing: terminate long-lived connections on a dedicated gateway fleet, keep a registry of who is connected where, persist each message once with a per-conversation sequence, and fan out asynchronously to online devices (push for the rest).

checks.label: Core messaging use case captured

tips.nudge: What is the one thing every user does in this app?
tips.hint: Write a functional requirement for sending a message to another user.
tips.show: F1: A user sends a text message to another user (1:1) and it is delivered to all of the recipient's devices.

checks.label: Conversations with more than two people

tips.nudge: The interviewer mentioned a member cap. For what?
tips.hint: Add group conversations and their size limit to scope.
tips.show: F2: Group chats of up to 200 members; a message to the group reaches every member.

checks.label: What happens when the recipient isn't connected

tips.nudge: The recipient's phone is in a drawer. Is the message lost?
tips.hint: Capture offline delivery and history across devices.
tips.show: F3: Messages are stored for 1 year; offline users get a push notification and catch up on reconnect, on any device.

checks.label: Delivery speed expectation stated

tips.nudge: What makes chat feel like chat rather than email?
tips.hint: State an end-to-end delivery target when both users are online.
tips.show: N1: Online-to-online delivery in < 500 ms at p99.

checks.label: Message throughput estimated

tips.nudge: Start from daily users and messages per user.
tips.hint: messages/day ÷ seconds in a day, then apply the peak factor.
tips.show: msgs_per_day = 50M × 40 = 2B; avg ≈ 23k /s, peak ≈ 70k /s.

checks.label: Concurrent connections estimated

tips.nudge: How many people hold the app open at the same moment?
tips.hint: daily users × the fraction connected at peak.
tips.show: concurrent = 50M × 1/5 = 10M open connections at peak.

checks.label: Storage for the retention period estimated

tips.nudge: How many messages pile up in a year, and how big is each?
tips.hint: messages/day × 365 × bytes per message (then replication on top).
tips.show: 2B × 365 × 200 B ≈ 146 TB/year before replication (~440 TB with 3 replicas).

checks.label: Sending interface defined

tips.nudge: What does the client transmit when the user taps send, and what does it get back?
tips.hint: Define the send operation (over the persistent connection or HTTP) with a client-generated id.
tips.show: WS frame / POST /conversations/{id}/messages {client_msg_id, text} → ack {message_id, seq, ts}

checks.label: Catch-up interface defined

tips.nudge: A phone reconnects after a flight. How does it get what it missed?
tips.hint: A GET that pages through a conversation from the last sequence number the device saw.
tips.show: GET /conversations/{id}/messages?after_seq=1234&limit=50 → [messages], next cursor

checks.label: Core data model defined

tips.nudge: What do you store for each message, and how is it found again?
tips.hint: Think about the access pattern: 'latest N messages of conversation X'.
tips.show: messages(conversation_id PK, seq CK, message_id, sender_id, body, created_at) in a wide-column store.

checks.label: Who belongs to which conversation modelled

tips.nudge: To deliver a group message you need to know who's in the group.
tips.hint: Model conversations and their members, plus each member's read position.
tips.show: conversation_members(conversation_id, user_id, joined_at, last_read_seq); user_conversations(user_id → conversation ids).

checks.label: Holding connections and routing to them designed as a part

tips.nudge: Alice is on one of hundreds of servers and Bob on another. That routing problem deserves its own part.
tips.hint: Add a part for the connection tier: compare broadcasting to all servers, hashing users to servers, and a lookup table of who is connected where.
tips.show: Part 'Connection tier and routing': WebSocket gateways behind an L4 LB; a Redis session registry device → gateway with a heartbeat TTL (also presence).

checks.label: Storing messages in a stable order designed as a part

tips.nudge: Two phones must show the same conversation in the same order, for a year. Which sub-problem is that?
tips.hint: Add a part for persistence and ordering: compare client timestamps, a global sequence and a per-conversation sequence, and pick a store for 'latest N of a conversation'.
tips.show: Part 'Message persistence and ordering': per-conversation seq (atomic counter), messages in Cassandra partitioned by conversation_id and clustered by seq, dedup by client_msg_id.

checks.label: Recipients without a connection handled as a part

tips.nudge: The phone is in a drawer, then a new laptop signs in. What do they each need?
tips.hint: Add a part for offline delivery: compare per-device inbox queues, data inside push payloads, and push-as-a-hint plus cursor sync.
tips.show: Part 'Offline delivery and catch-up': APNs/FCM wake-up push only; devices pull GET …/messages?after_seq= per changed conversation.

checks.label: Delivering to many members designed as a part

tips.nudge: A 200-member group turns one send into 200 deliveries. Who does that work, and does the sender wait?
tips.hint: Add a part for group fan-out: compare inline delivery, copying into every inbox, and async workers fed by a stream.
tips.show: Part 'Group fan-out': persist once, publish to Kafka keyed by conversation; fan-out workers look up members and gateways and deliver; the sender is acked after the write.

checks.label: Clients receive messages the moment they arrive

tips.nudge: The server must speak first when a message arrives. What does that need?
tips.hint: A fleet of servers whose only job is to hold open connections.
tips.show: WebSocket gateway fleet (~50k–100k connections each) behind a load balancer.

checks.label: Knowing which server holds a user's connection

tips.nudge: Alice is on gateway 17, Bob on gateway 203. How does a message find Bob?
tips.hint: Keep a lookup of user/device → gateway that gateways update on connect and disconnect.
tips.show: Session registry in Redis: device_id → gateway_id with a heartbeat TTL (doubles as presence).

checks.label: Fan-out decoupled from the sender's request

tips.nudge: A group message goes to 200 people. Should the sender wait for all of them?
tips.hint: Persist, ack the sender, and hand delivery to something asynchronous.
tips.show: Chat service → message stream (partitioned by conversation) → fan-out workers → recipients' gateways.

checks.label: Server-to-client delivery mechanism decided

tips.nudge: 10M clients polling every second is how many requests?
tips.hint: Compare short polling, long polling, server-sent events and WebSockets.
tips.show: WebSockets: bidirectional, one connection per device, server pushes instantly; long polling as fallback.

checks.label: Duplicates and gaps handled

tips.nudge: The network drops the ack and the phone sends the same message again. Then a worker crashes mid-delivery. What does each phone show?
tips.hint: Decide the delivery guarantee and how retries and missing messages are recognised.
tips.show: At-least-once delivery: the store ignores a repeated client_msg_id; clients drop a seq they already have and fetch any gap with after_seq.

checks.label: Failure scenarios walked through

tips.nudge: A gateway with 80k connections crashes. What happens next?
tips.hint: Cover gateway loss, fan-out worker lag and store unavailability.
tips.show: Clients reconnect with backoff+jitter to another gateway and sync from last seq; stream retains messages so workers replay; sender retries are deduped.

checks.label: Growth plan described

tips.nudge: Users double and groups grow to 5,000. What changes?
tips.hint: Think per tier: connections, routing, storage, fan-out.
tips.show: More gateways; shard registry; more stream partitions and store nodes; for huge groups switch to pull-on-open instead of per-member fan-out.
